title: yoga nidra
hook: a room of people lying flat on mats, and a teacher asks each of them for one short sentence

segments.voice: Yesterday, yoga nidra with Patanjali: even sleep is a movement of the mind.

Evening, a yoga studio, the lights low. A dozen people lie flat on their backs, arms a little away from the body, palms up. A blanket here and there. Someone's foot twitches. The teacher's voice is slow and even. Settle the body. Hear the sounds outside the room. Hear the sounds inside the room. Then comes an instruction that has nothing to do with relaxing. Make your resolve. A short sentence. Say it to yourself, three times, with feeling. Nobody else will hear it.
screen: `LIGHTS LOW. BODIES ON MATS.` → `HEAR THE SOUNDS OUTSIDE, THEN INSIDE.` → `MAKE YOUR RESOLVE.`

segments.voice: The guided form of yoga nidra was set out as a sequence by Swami Satyananda Saraswati of the Bihar School of Yoga, who says in his own book on the practice that he drew on older tantric practices of placing awareness in the body. In that book, the outline runs roughly like this. Settle the body in shavasana, the corpse pose. Make a resolve. Move awareness quickly around the body, part by part. Watch the breath. Feel pairs of opposites, heavy and light, hot and cold. Let images pass. Make the resolve again. Then come back slowly. The resolve has a Sanskrit name: sankalpa. It turned up at the start of the mantra sadhana, setting the terms of a practice, and it was at home on this path long before any studio. Before a puja, a Hindu priest or householder may make a sankalpa: a spoken statement of intention that names the time, the place, the person, and the purpose of the worship about to begin. This act is chosen, on purpose, by me, here. Satyananda carried the word into the practice, with some simple advice. Keep it short. Make it sincere. Say it at the start, while the mind is still clear, and again near the end, when the body is deeply at rest and the mind, in his account, is most receptive. So the practice isn't only lying still. It opens and closes with an intention, the way a puja does. Rest becomes something you walk into on purpose.
screen: `A SEQUENCE SHAPED AT THE BIHAR SCHOOL.` · `BODY, BREATH, OPPOSITES, IMAGES.` · `SANKALPA: THE RESOLVE BEFORE A PUJA.` · `SHORT, SINCERE, AT START AND END.` · then, large: `REST, WALKED INTO ON PURPOSE.`

segments.voice: Lie down, palms up, or sit back with the hands open, and hear the sounds furthest away, then the sounds in the room, then the breath. Let a short sentence form, something true you'd like to grow into, simple and in the present, and say it to yourself three times, unhurried. Then rest in the weight of the body, and near the end, if you like, say it once more.
Yoga nidra. The sleep of yoga, which in its guided form opens and closes with a sankalpa, a short, sincere resolve.
Your line: a short, sincere resolve. The same word that opens a puja. Until tomorrow.

howItsDone: In a guided yoga nidra session, people lie in shavasana while a teacher leads them through a resolve, a rotation of awareness through the body, the breath and images, then the resolve again; before a puja, a sankalpa states the time, place, person and purpose.

original.note: Sanskrit, in Devanagari: sankalpa, resolve, intention. Made before a puja, and at the start and end of yoga nidra.

chat.says: Why does our teacher ask for a resolve right in the middle of relaxing?
options: It's a sankalpa, an intention, like the one spoken before a puja.
It's a test to check that nobody in the room has fallen asleep.
It's a wish that the teacher promises will come true by morning.
chat.meaning: Satyananda's yoga nidra opens and closes with a sankalpa, a short, sincere resolve, the same word used before a puja.

Satyananda.meaning: Swami Satyananda Saraswati, who shaped guided yoga nidra

notes: Editor pass: review updated for 1022's new carry; the claim that studio yoga nidra 'today owes its shape' to Satyananda narrowed to what his own book says; sankalpa now acknowledged as met at the start of the mantra block (1012) instead of introduced as new; puja sankalpa 'often' softened to 'may'.

Attribution of the modern guided form to Swami Satyananda Saraswati and the Bihar School, and the link to older tantric practices (nyasa), is a historical claim not from a scripture; confirm wording. His book is under copyright and is only paraphrased; no dates are given on purpose.
The outline (shavasana, sankalpa, rotation of consciousness, breath, opposites, visualization, sankalpa, ending) is summarized from Satyananda's teaching; confirm order.
Satyananda's advice on the sankalpa (short, positive, repeated three times at start and end, said when the mind is receptive) is paraphrased; confirm.
The puja sankalpa (naming time, place, person, purpose) is described generally; customs vary by region and lineage.
The hook's 'a dozen people' is a scene detail, not a statistic.
Audit: removed 'then, he says, let it go, and don't keep checking on it' (teach and fork reveal); that advice could not be confirmed as Satyananda's and was attributed to him directly.
